summary: "A structure-guided framework shrinks long-term agent memory on two axes at once — consolidating related records into fewer retrieval units and re-encoding them into compact text — while keeping 99% of Mem0's original performance with half as many records."
image: "/assets/post-images/2026-11-22-memfolder-agent-memory-folding.svg"
---

Long-running agents accumulate a memory store that grows with every interaction, and the bill arrives twice. More records means higher retrieval overhead; longer retrieved context means more prefill compute and more decoding-time attention. Existing fixes split the problem in half: **pruning** drops records (and can throw away the evidence you needed) while **consolidation** merges them (and can produce fewer but *longer* retrieval units, so the token bill barely moves).

**MemFolder** (Zhejiang University and collaborators) attacks both halves at once by making record count and context length fall together, guided by structure that already exists across records.

The framework has two components that share the same memory groups. **RecordFolder** grounds entity mentions, then progressively selects anchors that are representative but complementary, and combines semantic affinity, entity affinity and temporal chaining to decide which records can be merged into a single retrieval unit without losing their joint meaning. **ContextFolder** then takes the original records inside a group and encodes them into compact text — with a verification feedback loop that rewrites the encoding when a key fact turns out not to be recoverable from it. In other words, the second stage isn't just compression; it's compression that is checked against retrieval and repaired when it fails.

**The headline result is on Mem0**, the strongest memory baseline in the comparison. On the three text benchmarks — **LoCoMo, PersonaMem and LongMemEval** — RecordFolder keeps **99.0% of the original average performance** while using **50% fewer records**, beating the strongest baseline by **1.9 percentage points in performance retention**. Stacked on top of ContextFolder, existing record-compression methods shorten their outputs further while retaining most of their accuracy.

Evaluation is not limited to text: the paper also reports results on two multimodal benchmarks, **M3-Bench-web** and **M3-Bench-robot** — the robot variant matters for a digest that follows embodied agents, where a memory record is not just text.

The angle worth keeping: most memory work optimizes retrieval quality and treats compression as an afterthought. MemFolder inverts that, treating the *structure* of the store — entities, affinity, temporal chains — as the signal that licenses compression, and then verifying the compressed form can still answer the question. Whether that holds up outside the two benchmark families is the open question; code is released at [github.com/xuyang-liu16/MemFolder](https://github.com/xuyang-liu16/MemFolder).

Source: [arXiv:2611.26427 — MemFolder: Structure-Guided Memory Folding for Efficient Agent Memory Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26427)
